title: Wedding Hashtag Ideas: 70 Examples and a Backup Plan
description: 70 wedding hashtag ideas from six formulas, how to check yours is unused, and why a hashtag misses private posts, plus the private backup that catches them.
dek: Six formulas, 70 examples and the honest truth about what a hashtag can collect.
excerpt: Last-name puns, merged names, dates and destinations: 70 wedding hashtag examples, a checklist to test yours, and what hashtags miss in 2026 (private accounts, stories).

faq.q: What makes a good wedding hashtag?
faq.a: A good wedding hashtag is short (under about 20 characters), easy to spell after hearing it once, and not already used by another couple. Puns on your last name, your first names plus a phrase, or your names plus the year all work. Capitalize each word so it’s easy to read, and leave out punctuation, which breaks hashtags.

faq.q: How do you make a wedding hashtag with your last name?
faq.a: Look for a phrase that already contains your last name or something that sounds like it: Stone gives #SetInStone, Hart gives #HappilyEverHart, Knott gives #TyingTheKnotts. If your name is very common or hard to pun on, add a twist instead: “Meet the,” “Officially the” or the year, as in #MeetTheSmiths2027.

They work for finding public posts, and they’re fun on signs. They miss a lot of wedding photos, though: posts from private accounts don’t appear on hashtag pages, stories disappear after 24 hours, and Instagram no longer lets you follow a hashtag. Use one alongside a private shared album or guest camera, not instead of it.

faq.q: How long should a wedding hashtag be?
faq.a: Aim for under 20 characters and treat 25 as the limit. Guests type it from a sign, often in dim light with a drink in the other hand, so every extra word is a chance to misspell it. If your favorite idea runs long, shorten the names to initials or drop the filler words.

faq.q: Can you see wedding hashtag posts from private accounts?
faq.a: Not through the hashtag. Instagram says that when a private account adds a hashtag, the post won’t appear on that hashtag’s page. You’ll see it only if you already follow that person, in your own feed. So a hashtag alone can miss many of your guests’ photos, which is why a private album or shared camera works better for collecting them.
